title: The alarm that didn't stop the landing

probes.question: What did the Apollo computer do when it became overloaded?
options: Dropped low-priority tasks and kept critical ones running

probes.question: True or false: the 1202 alarm forced Apollo 11 to abort the landing.

image.alt: The Apollo 11 lunar landing mission crew, pictured from left to right, Neil A. Armstrong, commander; Michael Collins, command module pilot; and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr., lunar module pilot.

panels.text: 20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin are descending toward the Moon in the lunar module Eagle, guided by the Apollo Guidance Computer.
Minutes before landing, the computer flashes alarms numbered 1202 and 1201. They are unexpected.
In Houston, guidance officer Steve Bales, advised by Jack Garman, has to decide quickly: abort or continue?
The twist: the computer was overloaded, but it had been designed to drop lower-priority tasks and keep the critical ones running. Bales said go, and Eagle landed.
